reasoning: Empirically `ip addr` printed `inet 127.0.0.1/8 scope host lo` and `inet 172.17.0.2/16` — prefix length, no dotted-decimal mask. `ifconfig` on the same host prints `netmask 255.255.0.0`, which is the contrast the text draws.

claim: ARP never crosses a router: an entry for an off-subnet address will always be the router's MAC, not the remote host's.
reasoning: The conclusion is right but the mechanism as written is wrong and misleads about what `ip neigh` contains. A host performs next-hop determination first (RFC 1122 section 3.3.1): for an off-subnet destination it resolves the gateway's address, so no neighbour entry for the off-subnet address is created at all. `ip neigh` on the test host listed only the on-link gateway, not any off-subnet destination. Reworded to say the host does not resolve the off-subnet address at all and the frame instead carries the router's MAC.

claim: A PTR record for 192.0.2.10 lives at `10.2.0.192.in-addr.arpa`; a CNAME cannot coexist with other record types at the same name so cannot sit at a zone apex; an MX must point to a name with an A or AAAA record, not a CNAME.

claim: A TCP header is at least 20 bytes and carries sequence and acknowledgement numbers, flags and a receive window; a UDP header is exactly 8 bytes: source port, destination port, length, checksum.
reasoning: RFC 9293's TCP header format is five mandatory 32-bit rows — source/destination port, sequence number, acknowledgment number, Data Offset plus reserved plus control bits plus window, and checksum plus urgent pointer — i.e. 160 bits, 20 bytes, before any options, and Data Offset is defined as "the number of 32-bit words in the TCP header". RFC 768's header diagram is four 16-bit fields — source port, destination port, length, checksum — i.e. exactly 8 bytes, with no options. Both fetched and read directly.
source: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9293.txt header format and Data Offset definition; https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc768.txt (both fetched)

claim: `tcpdump` captures and prints packets showing the handshake flags; `-i IFACE` chooses an interface, `-n` skips name resolution, and a filter expression such as `port 443` narrows the capture. Example `tcpdump -n port 443`. `[S]`, `[S.]` and `[.]` mark SYN, SYN-ACK and ACK. It needs elevated privilege.
reasoning: `man tcpdump` documents `-i interface`/`--interface=interface`, `-n` ("Don't convert addresses ... port numbers"), the filter expression as a trailing argument, and states that the tcpflags are "some combination of S (SYN), F (FIN), P (PSH), R (RST), U (URG)" with the note "The `.' means the ACK" — so `[S.]` is SYN plus ACK. The man page also states that capturing requires special privileges.

claim: The closing side holds the connection in TIME_WAIT for twice the maximum segment lifetime.
reasoning: RFC 9293 uses the literal quantity "2 MSL" for the TIME-WAIT timeout throughout — the connection-close diagrams annotate the closing side's wait as "(2 MSL)", and the event-processing rules say "Remain in the TIME-WAIT state. Restart the 2 MSL time-wait timeout." Fetched and grepped.

Empirically `ss -tl` (no `-n`) printed `127.0.0.1:ssh` — port translated, address still numeric — while `netstat -tl` printed `localhost:ssh`, translating both. The blanket phrase "no name resolution"/"without resolving names or service names" overstates what `-n` does in ss. Narrowed the prose to ports and service names.
source: man ss and ss --help (iproute2 6.1.0); empirical comparison of `ss -tl`/`ss -tln` and `netstat -tl`/`netstat -tln` in container

Empirically `ss -tlp` as root printed `users:(("nc",pid=1755,fd=3))` for a socket, and the Local Address column showed `127.0.0.1:2222` distinct from a wildcard bind.

claim: A 502 or 503 comes from a proxy in front of the application, not from the application itself.
reasoning: RFC 9110 section 15.6.3 defines 502 (Bad Gateway) as the server "while acting as a gateway or proxy" receiving an invalid response from an inbound server, and section 15.6.5 defines 504 (Gateway Timeout) the same way. But section 15.6.4 defines 503 (Service Unavailable) as the server itself being "currently unable to handle the request due to a temporary overload or scheduled maintenance" — nothing about a gateway or proxy. 503 is routinely emitted by the origin application. Corrected the pair to 502 and 504.

claim: `firewall-cmd --list-all` shows everything configured in the active zone; `--zone=NAME` inspects another zone and `--list-all-zones` shows every zone.
reasoning: `--zone=NAME` and `--list-all-zones` are correct (`man firewall-cmd` lists `[--permanent] [--zone=zone] [--policy=policy] --list-all` and `[--permanent] --list-all-zones`). Corrected in the prose, the Commands table and the section scenario.

reasoning: `man firewall-cmd` documents `--add-port=portid[-portid]/protocol`, `--add-service=service`, `--permanent`, `--reload` and `--zone=zone`, and opens with "The runtime configuration in firewalld is separated from the permanent configuration", with `--reload` reloading the permanent configuration into the runtime one.

reasoning: On the Ubuntu 24.04 test system the binary identifies itself as `iptables v1.8.10 (nf_tables)` in its own error output, i.e. the nft backend rather than the legacy one.

claim: `nc -zv host port` tests whether a port accepts a connection without sending data; `-z` scan only, `-v` report the outcome, `-w SECS` shorten the timeout, `-u` test UDP. It reports "succeeded" or "Connection refused" or hangs until timeout. Example `nc -zv web01.example.com 443`.
reasoning: `man nc` documents `-z  Only scan for listening daemons, without sending any data to them`, `-v  Produce more verbose output`, `-w timeout` and `-u  Use UDP instead of TCP`. Empirically `nc -zv example.com 443` printed "Connection to example.com (172.66.147.243) 443 port [tcp/https] succeeded!" and `nc -zv 127.0.0.1 9` printed "nc: connect to 127.0.0.1 port 9 (tcp) failed: Connection refused".
source: man nc (netcat-openbsd, Ubuntu 24.04); empirical runs in container

claim: `ping` sends ICMP echo requests and reports replies; `-c N` stops after N packets, `-i` sets the interval, `-W` the reply timeout, `-4`/`-6` force the address family. Example `ping -c 4 www.example.com`.
reasoning: `man ping` documents `-c count`, `-i interval`, `-W timeout` ("Time to wait for a response, in seconds"), and `-4` / `-6`. Empirically `ping -c 2 127.0.0.1` produced the loss statistics block described.
source: man ping (iputils, Ubuntu 24.04); empirical run in container

claim: A ping that fails with "Name or service not known" is a DNS failure rather than a reachability failure, and the output states this plainly.
reasoning: Empirically `ping -c 1 nosuchhost.invalid` printed exactly `ping: nosuchhost.invalid: Name or service not known` and sent no packets.
source: empirical run in Ubuntu 24.04 container (iputils ping)

claim: ICMP echo request is type 8 and echo reply type 0; destination unreachable is type 3 and time exceeded type 11, and ICMP carries no ports.
reasoning: RFC 792 was fetched and read: the Destination Unreachable Message section gives Type 3, the Time Exceeded Message section gives Type 11, and the Echo or Echo Reply Message section gives "8 for echo message; 0 for echo reply message". None of the ICMP message formats contains a port field.

claim: `traceroute` prints the route packets take; `-I` ICMP probes, `-T` TCP probes, `-n` numeric, `-m` max hops (30 by default), `-p` destination port base. Example `traceroute -n www.example.com`. The default method is UDP to unlikely high ports.
reasoning: `man traceroute` documents `-I, --icmp`, `-T, --tcp`, `-n`, `-m max_ttl, --max-hops=max_ttl` with "The default is 30", and `-p port, --port=port` with "For UDP tracing, specifies the destination port base traceroute will use". The default method section reads "The traditional, ancient method of tracerouting. Used by default. Probe packets are udp datagrams with so-called 'unlikely' destination ports."

claim: `tracepath` traces the path and discovers the path MTU; `-n` numeric, `-m` max hops, and it needs no elevated privilege and deliberately has few options.
reasoning: `man tracepath` documents `-n`, `-m`, and states "it does not require superuser privileges" while describing path MTU discovery as part of its output. Its documented option list is short, matching the "few options" characterisation.

claim: `mtr` combines ping and traceroute into a continuously updating per-hop report; `-r` report mode for a fixed run, `-n` numeric, `-c` cycle count. Example `mtr -r -c 100 www.example.com`.
reasoning: `man mtr` documents `-r, --report`, `-n, --no-dns` and `-c COUNT, --report-cycles COUNT`, so the flags and their pairing with long forms are as stated.

claim: `ip` is divided into objects — `ip addr` layer 3, `ip link` layer 2, `ip route` routing table, `ip neigh` ARP/neighbour cache — each taking subcommands, `show` by default, plus `add`, `del` and `set`. Examples `ip addr show`, `ip link set dev enp0s3 up`, `ip route`.
reasoning: Verified empirically for all four objects in the container: bare invocations behaved as `show`, `ip route get` and `ip neigh help` printed the documented subcommand grammar including add/del/change/replace, and `man ip-link` documents `ip link set dev DEVICE up|down`.
source: man ip, man ip-link, man ip-address, man ip-route, ip neigh help; empirical runs in container

claim: `ifconfig` is legacy net-tools interface configuration and display; `-a` includes inactive interfaces and `IFACE up`/`down` changes state. It is deprecated and absent by default on many current distributions.
reasoning: `man ifconfig` documents `-a  display all interfaces which are currently available, even if down`, and the keywords `up  This flag causes the interface to be activated` and `down  This flag causes the driver for this interface to be shut down`. net-tools was not present at all on this Mac host's Linux-tool equivalents and had to be present in the image explicitly, consistent with the deprecation claim.

claim: `ss -tulpn` and `netstat -tulpn` take the same option letters and produce comparable output, and `-n` is numeric so ports and addresses are not translated into names.
reasoning: The shared letters are real: `netstat --help` prints `-r, --route`, `-i, --interfaces`, `-n, --numeric`, `-p, --programs`, `-l, --listening`, and both `ss -tulpn` and `netstat -tulpn` ran and produced the same shape of output. The `-n` description is wrong for `ss`. Empirically `ss -tl` printed `127.0.0.1:ssh` (address already numeric) while `netstat -tl` printed `localhost:ssh`; `man ss` defines `-n` as "Do not try to resolve service names" and provides a separate `-r, --resolve` to resolve addresses at all, whereas `man netstat` says without `--numeric` "the socket address is resolved to its canonical host name (FQDN), and the port number is translated into the corresponding service name". Split the sentence so each tool's behaviour is stated correctly.
source: man ss, man netstat, netstat --help; empirical comparison of `ss -tl`/`ss -tln` and `netstat -tl`/`netstat -tln` in container

claim: `netstat -tulpn` is the same view from legacy net-tools; `-r` prints the routing table and `-i` interface statistics.
reasoning: `netstat --help` prints `-r, --route  display routing table` and `-i, --interfaces  display interface table`. Empirically `netstat -tulpn` printed the "Active Internet connections (only servers)" table with the Proto/Local Address/State/PID columns described.
source: netstat --help and man netstat (net-tools, Ubuntu 24.04); empirical run in container

claim: `ss` reads socket information from the kernel through netlink, whereas `netstat` parses files under `/proc/net`, which is why `ss` is markedly faster on hosts with many connections. Dropping `-n` makes the output translate 22 into `ssh` via `/etc/services`.
reasoning: `man netstat` FILES lists `/proc/net/tcp`, `/proc/net/udp`, `/proc/net/unix` etc. as the sources it reads, and `/etc/services` as the translation file. ss is part of iproute2 and uses the sock_diag netlink interface; `man ss` refers to netlink socket families throughout. Empirically `ss -tl` and `netstat -tl` both rendered port 22 as `ssh` and `-n` restored `22` in each.
source: man netstat (FILES section), man ss; empirical run in container

claim: `dig +short` prints only the answer data and can be combined with a type: `dig +short example.com MX`.
reasoning: `man dig` documents `+short, +noshort`. Empirically `dig +short example.com` returned only the two A record values and `dig example.com MX +short` returned only `0 .`, with no status, TTL or answering-server lines — which is the loss the text warns about when diagnosing.
source: man dig; empirical runs in container

claim: `dig` and `nslookup` bypass `/etc/hosts` and the name service switch entirely, so they show what DNS says and not what an application will get; `getent hosts` is the tool for the latter.
reasoning: dig and nslookup construct DNS queries and send them to a nameserver (dig's man page describes it as "a flexible tool for interrogating DNS name servers"), while `man getent` states that getent looks up entries in the administrative databases through the Name Service Switch, whose `hosts:` line on the test system is `files dns`. The two therefore consult different sources by construction.
source: man dig; man getent; /etc/nsswitch.conf on Ubuntu 24.04

claim: `curl -v` shows the full request and response exchange, and can be combined with `-I` or `-o /dev/null`; `-m` sets a timeout.
reasoning: `man curl` documents `-v, --verbose`, `-o, --output <file>` and `-m, --max-time <fractional seconds>`, all of which combine freely with `-I, --head`.

claim: `wget` downloads a URL to a file; `-O FILE` chooses the output file (`-O -` for stdout), `-q` is quiet, `-r` recursive. Unlike curl it writes a file by default.
reasoning: `man wget` documents `-O file, --output-document=file`, `-q, --quiet` and `-r, --recursive`, and describes wget's default behaviour as saving the retrieved document to a local file — the contrast with curl writing to standard output.

claim: A `curl` exit status of 0 means the transfer completed, not that the HTTP status was 2xx — `--fail` makes an HTTP error a non-zero exit.
reasoning: `man curl` documents `-f, --fail` as failing silently on server errors so that curl returns a non-zero exit code for an HTTP error response, which by implication is not the default behaviour.

claim: Quick reference row: `tcpdump -i` selects the interface and tcpdump needs elevated privilege; it observes traffic and never changes configuration.
reasoning: `man tcpdump` documents `-i interface, --interface=interface` and states that capturing requires special privileges (reading a saved capture file does not). tcpdump has no rule- or address-modifying options; it is a capture and print tool.

claim: Predictable names use a two-character type prefix (`en` Ethernet, `wl` wireless LAN, `ww` wireless WAN, `ib` InfiniBand, `sl` serial line IP) plus a location suffix — `o<index>` onboard, `s<slot>` hotplug slot, `p<bus>s<slot>` PCI location, `x<MAC>` — so `enp0s3` is Ethernet, PCI bus 0, slot 3; the scheme is disabled with `net.ifnames=0`.
reasoning: systemd.net-naming-scheme(7) Table 1 lists exactly these prefixes — en Ethernet, ib InfiniBand, sl Serial line IP (slip), wl Wireless local area network (WLAN), ww Wireless wide area network (WWAN) — and the property tables give `prefix o number` PCI on-board index, `prefix x AABBCCDDEEFF` from the MAC, `prefix [P domain] s slot [f function]` for the hotplug slot, and `prefix [P domain] p bus s slot [f function]` labelled "PCI geographical location". systemd-udevd.service(8) documents `net.ifnames=`: "Network interfaces are renamed to give them predictable names when possible. It is enabled by default; specifying 0 disables it."
source: https://www.freedesktop.org/software/systemd/man/latest/systemd.net-naming-scheme.html and https://www.freedesktop.org/software/systemd/man/latest/systemd-udevd.service.html (both fetched and grepped; dataset source id systemd-net-naming-scheme)

claim: `ip link` lists the interfaces this system actually has with their names and state; `show` is the default and `set dev NAME up`/`down` changes state. Example `ip link`.
reasoning: Empirically bare `ip link` listed `lo`, `tunl0@NONE` and `eth0@if21` with flags and state, identical to `ip link show`. `man ip-link` documents the `set dev DEVICE up|down` form.
source: man ip-link; empirical run in container
